newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico govt's surprise rail stake alarms analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico govt's surprise rail stake alarms analysts.

text.p: The Mexican government's intervention in the recently privatized Northeast Railway raises serious questions about the government's plans to sell off state assets, analysts said on Friday.
"This is not what I'd call a privatization," said one New York analyst who declined to be named.

The government on Thursday night said it would take back a temporary stake of up to 24.5 percent in the 50-year rail operating concession it awarded in full in December to a joint venture of Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) and Kansas City Southern Industries.
The concession, which cost $1.4 billion, was for 80 percent of the railway's assets.

In addition to the new 24.5 percent stake in the joint venture, the government still holds the remaining 20 percent of the railway's assets. That would give it what analysts estimated was a 39.6 percent stake in the railway as a whole.
The announcement of the increased government participation took not only Wall Street analysts but also spokesmen within the companies by surprise.

Spokesmen for TMM and Kansas City Southern, joined through concession company Transportacion Ferroviaria Mexicana (TFM), said they did not know precisely why the government took a bigger equity stake than had been expected.

"TMM and its associates announced that because of the strategic character of the railroad route for economic development and foreign trade to the country, the federal government decided to participate as a member of TFM," said TMM's press statement on Thursday.

The only clue to the mystery came in a Communications and Transport Ministry press statement Thursday night. It said that "to assure healthy development of (Northeast Railway), a plan has been designed that allows it to have a better financial position and sufficient working capital to face investment needs established in its business plan."
Government spokesmen could not be reached for comment.

"The fact that the government is going to buy a stake does not hurt the companies as such, but it could appear that the government lacks seriousness in that it changes schemes at the last minute," said another analyst who asked not to be named.

The government announced it was retaining the 24.5 percent stake in the concession the night before TFM was due to make its first payment for the railway. TFM said it would make that 4.429 billion peso payment on Friday.
Other analysts were reluctant to comment, saying they had received pressure to keep quiet about the matter.

A string of Mexico's privatizations have turned sour, including the Chihuahua-Pacifico Railway, when offers failed to reach the minimum bid. In petrochemicals, plans to sell a majority stake were reversed at the last minute because of political opposition.

"It is more or less normal that there are problems with privatizations, especially because the most attractive assets have already been sold off," said Pedro Javier Gonzalez, chief economist at the Mexican Institute of Political Studies. "It does indicate that the government is not being able to do things the way it would have liked."
"We would see it as a positive development for TMM," said Bear Stearns analyst Santiago Pique in a report before the rumors of the government's intervention were confirmed.
"It would reduce the amount of the total price tag that TMM would have to contribute from $686 million to $520.8 million with the resulting saving in interest expense," he said.
Analysts had been concerned that the railway's expense would reduce TMM and Kansas City's earnings. Pique added that the additional partner would help reduce the railway's risk.
Analysts estimated the government's participation would reduce TMM and Kansas City Southern's participation in the railroad holding company to about 37 percent each.
